sections.overview: The Meadow Pipit is a small, ground-feeding songbird of open country, breeding across northern Eurasia and wintering farther south. It is plain-looking at first glance, but its calls and streaking help separate it from several similar pipits.
sections.identification: It is about 15 cm long, with a wingspan near 25 cm; a French aerodrome guide gives a typical mass of 18 g, ranging from 11 to 25 g. Adults are brown to olive above, with dark streaks, a pale open-looking face, a fine bill, pale pinkish legs, and a long hind claw. Dark streaks continue from the breast down the flanks, while the rump is fairly plain; the sexes look alike in plumage. In BTO samples, male wing chord and mass averaged 83.2 mm and 19.2 g, versus 77.7 mm and 18.5 g in females (sample averages, not a visual sex test). The Tree Pipit (Anthus trivialis) is a close lookalike, but its flank streaks are finer than its breast streaks, and it usually has a stronger bill and more marked face; calls are often the safest clue.
sections.habitat: During breeding it favors open, often damp country: moorland, bogs, heaths, rough grassland, marshes and saltmarshes. Northern populations move south in autumn to spend winter in western and southern Europe, around the Mediterranean and in North Africa; some British and western European birds remain year-round.
sections.diet: It searches low vegetation and bare ground for small invertebrates, especially insects and their larvae; spiders and worms are also taken. Seeds may supplement the diet, particularly outside the breeding season.
sections.behavior: Most feeding takes place on the ground, and after breeding the birds often gather into flocks. A displaying male rises while singing, then descends in a fluttering or parachuting glide back toward the grass.
sections.reproduction: The breeding season varies with latitude, broadly from March to August. The female hides a cup-shaped grass-and-moss nest beneath a tussock or low shrub and usually lays four or five eggs; she incubates them, and both parents feed the chicks.
sections.ecology: It is often confused with other small, streaked pipits, especially the Tree Pipit in summer and the Water Pipit in winter. Compare several traits together—streaking, face pattern, bill, leg color, habitat, season and call—because no single plumage mark is always decisive.
sections.conservation: The BTO reports a 19% fall in the UK breeding population from 1995 to 2024. The same source currently lists the species as globally Near Threatened. BirdLife’s assessment history records Least Concern in 2021, after Near Threatened assessments in 2015–2018.
